National Textbook Council 
*102. SHRIMATI HEMA MALINI: 
SHRI R.S. GAVAI:† 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Central Advisory Board of Education 
(CABE) Committee had recommended for setting up of a National Textbook 
Council; 
(b) if so, the details of its recommendations; and 
(c) the action Government propose to take in this regards? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) to (c) A Statement '- 
laid on the Table of the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The recommendations are:— 
(i) There be instituted a National Textbook Council (NTC) to monitor 
textbooks. This must be independent of any organization involved in 
textbook preparation, and also be fully autonomous so as genuinely 
to represent civil society and academia. 
†The Question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri R.S. Gaval. 

RAJYA SABHA                     [1 August, 2005] 
(ii)  The CABE may set up a Standing Committee, which would be guided 
by the NTC. The Standing Committee should be empowered to prepare the 
guidelines and outline the parameters for periodic reviews of the 
textbooks, to be completed within six months of the beginning of the 
academic session. Review would exam ine social content of books as 
well as assess their standards, relevance and suitability for the age group. 
These periodic reviews should be submitted to the government, and 
widely publicized through the media. 
(c) The recommendations are under examination. 
SHRI R.S. GAVAI: Mr. Chairman, Si r, at the outset, I welcome the 
decision of the Government, but my supplementary is, keeping in view the damage 
which caused spreading of caste and creed, and all mythological things under the 
garb of history, whether the Government will implement the recommendation 
immediately and how much time the Government will take in this respect?

SHRI URKHAO GWRA BRAHMA: Sir, it is good that a number of 
projects are going on in the Bodoland area of Assam under the Special 
Financial Package. But I would like to know from the hon. Minister one thing. 
What is the mechanism for monitoring of works and who is responsible for the 
maintenance of quality of works? Whether the Ministry is satisfied with the 
progress of implementation of works. 
SHRI P.R. KYNDIAH: Mr. Chairman, Si r, in so far as the monitoring 
system is concerned, we have two types of mechanism. One is the State 
Government of Assam itself, and the other is at our level, at the Ministry level. 
In fact, our Secretary had been to Assam just for that matter, that is, firstly, to 
speed up the release of funds; secondly, to monitor the quality of works, and 
thirdly, to see how far the work has been done. So, we are quite aware of this, 
and it is important that we need to see how far the progress has been achieved. 
SHRI URKHAO GWRA BRAHMA: Sir, my second supplementary is, the 
Bodoland area is flood-prone. To bring about infrastructural development of the area 
and in view of the threat posed by floods, a sum of Rs. 500 crore is not 
sufficient. I would like to know from the hon. Minister whether

Proclamation of Sunni Wakf Board of U.P. 
105. SHRIMATI BIMBA RAIKAR:† 
SHRI DATTA MEGHE: 
Will the Minister of CULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are keeping a close watch on the proclamation of the 
Sunni Wakf Board of U.P. certifying the historic monument Taj Mahal as a Wakf 
property; 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shrimati Bimba Raikar. 
9 

RAJYA SABHA [1 August, 2005] 
(b) whether Government propose to challenge the claim in a higher court 
of law; and 
(c) whether anticipating a spate of such claims to historic monuments 
elsewhere in the country as Wakf property, Centre would pre-empt such claims 
through an Ordinance? 
THE MINISTER OF CULTURE (SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY): (a) to (c) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The claim of the U.P. Sunni Central Wakf Board over 
the Taj Mahal as Wakf property will be challenged in the Supreme Court by 
way of a Special Leave Petition. 
(c) No, Sir. There is no such proposal at present. 
SHRIMATI BIMBA RAIKAR: Sir, the U.P. Sunni Wakf Board claims that Taj 
Mahal belongs to them and that is a challenge to the authority of the Indian 
Government which administers the national monuments through the 
Archaeological Survey of India. If the Government has no control on the Wakf Boards, 
tomorrow they may say that the Red Fort also belongs to them and the Wakf Boards 
of each and every State will demand the administration of the monuments in the 
States. Taj Mahal is not a place of worship where pilgrims go. It is open to everybody and 
to all castes and creeds. It is a national monument. I would like to know the reaction of the 
Government to this. 
SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY: Sir, th e claim of Sunni Wakf Board is 
untenable, ridiculous and baseless, both from historical angle and legal angle.

DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Indira Gandhi National Open University (IGNOU) was 
established under an Act of Parliament and hence all universities in the country

established by an Act of Parliament (No. 50 of 1985) and the degrees/ 
diplomas/certificates awarded by it are treated equivalent to the corresponding 
awards of other Universities in the country. The University Grants Commission 
has issued instructions on the subject from time to time.

Amritsar, it is yet to recognize the MCA degree of IGNOU. Universities being 
autonomous, mutual recognition and equivalence of awards are decided by 
each University in accordance with its Statutes. The Association of Indian 
Universities encourages the practice of  reciprocal recognition of Degrees by 
Universities.

THE MINISTER OF CULTURE (SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY): (a) to (d) It is a 
fact that Jama Masjid is a historic monument and deserves to be properly 
conserved. A PIL was filed in the hon'ble High Court of Delhi seeking 
declaration of Jama Masjid as a centrally protected monument on 12.10.2004. 
In compliance with the orders of the Hon'ble High Court dated 3.11.2004, a

General, Archaeological Survey of India which was attended by the officials from 
the Delhi Wakf Board on the subject of declaring Jama Masjid as a monument 
of national importance. The consensus in the meeting was to continue the present 
system wherein Archaeological Survey of India would undertake conservation 
works of Jama Masjid in view of its historical and archaeological importance 
but without taking it over as a protected monument under the Ancient 
Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958. 
The Delhi High Court in their interim order dated 26.5.2005 came to the finding 
that the notification issued by the Government of India dated April 16,1970 
shows Jama Masjid built by Mughal Emperor, Shahjahan as one of the Wakf 
properties. It was further directed that if any repairs have to be carried out by the 
Archaeological Survey of India, the same shall be done in consultation with the 
Wakf Board in view of the aforesaid position. 
The hon'ble High Court of Delhi has further directed in their interim order dated 
14.7.2005 that the Municipal Corporation of Delhi and Delhi Wakf Board with 
the assistance from the Police should remove the unauthorized structures from and 
around the Wakf land. The Survey Commissioner (Wakf) should carry out 
survey and identify unauthorized structures inside and outside the monument on 
Wakf land. On the subject of conservation and repairs of the Jama Masjid, it has 
been directed by the Hon'ble Court that small repairs of urgent nature should be 
carried out by the Archaeological Survey of India and a report should be filed 
by the next date of hearing which is on 3rd August, 2005. For the long-term 
repairs, the Archaeological Survey of India should do the necessary exercise and 
inform the cost involved to the Delhi Wakf Board. Further, the matter is 
subjudice in the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi.

658. SHRI K.B. KRISHNA MURTHY: SHRI 
SANTOSH BAGRODIA: SHRI 
HARISH RAWAT: 
Will the Minister of HEAVY INDUSTRIES AND PUBLIC ENTERPRISES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to implement good corporate governance 
standards in the Central PSE; 
59 

RAJYA SABHA [1 August, 2005] 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; 
(d) whether the Government have taken a view on the recommendations of 
various Committees on corporate governance; 
(e) if so, the details of the action taken so far; and 
(f) if no action has been taken so far, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF HEAVY INDUSTRIES 
AND PUBLIC ENTERPRISES (SHRI SONTOSH MOHAN DEV): (a) to (f) To 
implement good corporate governance standards in the Central PSEs, the 
Government issue guidelines from time to time on Professionalisation of Board 
of Directors. While issuing these guidelines, Government also take into 
consideration the recommendations/reports of various Committees. Further, 
the Government have asked the listed CPSEs and their administrative Ministries 
to follow the guidelines of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) on 
corporate governance. Navratna and Miniratna schemes also provide for setting 
up of Audit Committee by the Board of Directors of these PSEs.

Purchase preference policy 
661. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of HEAVY INDUSTRIES 
AND PUBLIC ENTERPRISES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether extension of the purchase preference policy by another 
three years for the Central Public Sector Undertaking would help the loss- 
making units or the benefit would accrue only to already profit-making 
PSUs; 
(b) the percentage of business contracted by PSUs that is 
attributable to the purchase preference policy during the years 2003 
and 2004; and 
(c) whether Government propose any measures which would gradually 
made them profit-making in the foreseable future as loss-making or nearly 
sick PSUs require special consideration? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF HEAVY INDUSTRIES 
AND PUBLIC ENTERPRISES (SHRI SONTOSH MOHAN DEV): (a) 
Government has extended the Purchase Preference Policy (PPP) for another 3 
years i.e. upto 31.3.2008. The PPP is a general policy capable of benefiting both 
loss making and profit earning Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs). 
However, while extending the PPP upto 31.3.2008, Government have directed 
the administrative Ministries/Departments in charge of CPSEs to identify such 
CPSEs as may or may not require the support of PPP. 
(b) As per information available, the percentage of orders received by 
CPSEs under PPP during 2002-03 an d 2003-04 was about 0.40% and 
0.49% respectively of the turnover of the beneficiary CPSEs during the 
respective years. 
(c) Enterprises specific measures are taken by the concerned 
administrative Ministries/Departments/CPSEs from time to time in this 
regard. Some measures include periodical review of performance, financial 
and business restructuring, modernization, upgradation of technology, 
infusion of fresh funds, rightsizing of manpower, purchase, preference, 
improved marketing strategy, cost control measures etc. 
75

H.M.T. Units in NER 
662. SHRI DWIJENDRA NATH SHARMAH: Will the Minister of HEAVY 
INDUSTRIES AND PUBLIC ENTERPRISES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether H.M.T. has any factory or installation in Assam and N.E. 
Region; 
(b) if so, whether these are running properly; 
(c) if not, the reasons of their closure; and 
(d) the steps Government propose to close such installation and industry in N.E. 
Region? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF HEAVY INDUSTRIES 
AND PUBLIC ENTERPRISES (SHRI SONTOSH MOHAN DEV): (a) and (b) 
No, Sir. At present, HMT Ltd. and its subsidiaries do not have any factory or 
installation in Assam and N.E. Region. N.P.(c) and (d) HMT Ltd. had a Miniature 
Battery Unit at Guwahati, Assam Manufacturing Button type of cells for quartz 
watches. As a part of Turnaround Plan of HMT, in 2000 it was decided to close 
down five unviable and chronically loss making units including Miniature Battery 
Unit at Guwahati, Assam. This unit was closed on 31.12.2000 by giving VRS to 
the employees. The land on which it was situated has been taken over by Assam 
Industrial Development Corporation. 
Autonomy to Universities 
663. SHRI K. RAMA MOHAN RAO: W ill the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Central Advisory Board of Education's First 
Report recommended for autonomy to the Universities to start self-financing 
courses; 
(b) if so, whether the Report has been discussed within his Ministry; 
(c) the other recommendations made by the CABE with regard to 
University education; 
(d) whether it is also a fact that CABE strongly recommended that 1/3rd of 
the investment should go to higher education; and 
76 

[1 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(e) if so, what is the investment made in higher education during the last 
five years? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALIASHRAF FATMI): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. 
The report states that all universities and colleges should have the autonomy to start 
self-financing courses, particularly in new and emerging areas where job 
opportunities exist subject to the over-all framework provided by the funding and 
regulatory bodies. Rules and regulations on this may be reviewed with a view to 
dispensing with avoidable hassles. 
(c) Other major recommendations contained in the report of the Central 
Advisory Board of Education Committee (CABE) on Autonomy of Higher 
Education Institutions are detailed in the Statement enclosed. (See below). 
(d) Yes, Sir. 
(e) A sum of Rs. 2737.04 crore and Rs. 5435.83 crore under Plan and Non-
Plan respectively was provided to the UGC during the last 5 years. 
Statement 
Main recommendations contained in the Report of the Central Advisory 
Board of Education (CABE) Committeee on Autonomy of Higher 
Education Institutions 
1. Formulation of a Central Legislation in consultation with UGC, AICTE and 
other Professional Councils to streamline establishment and governance 
of Private Universities, Deemed to  be Universities, Self-Financing 
Institutions and establishment of Foreign Universities in India. 
2. National Testing Service (NTS) on th e lines of Educational Testing 
Service of USA for the purpose of setting up national norms of students 
performance. 
3. Approach Planning Commission for the enhancement of allocation to 
higher education sector to the level of 2% of GDP. 
4. Set up a task force to re-examine the existing UGC Act to provide for 
incorporation of new provisions to suit the emerging concerns and 
realities of higher education. 
77 

RAJYA SABHA [1 August, 2005] 
5. To promote Job Oriented Courses. 
6. Set up norms of accreditation, which could be profitably employed by 
the non-governmental agencies. 
7. To provide a forum to national level teacher's organization to develop norms 
for teacher appraisal. 
8. Undertake revision of UGC Act to make it a more significant instrument. 
9. Set up a consortium of institutions involving other statutory bodies, 
industries and research laboratories to work out details for necessary 
collaboration in enhancing activities of research. 
 
10. Evolve strategies to monitor the proper utilization of grants made 
available to the institutions of higher education and to seek from the 
institutions the outcomes of the programmes. 
11. The universities and institutions of higher education should immediately 
initiate steps to review their Act, St atutes & Ordinances to provide for 
greater autonomy in consultation with respective Governments. 
12. Grant autonomy to individual institutions in matters of design of 
curriculum 
13. Set up an Internal Qualtiy Assurance Cell. 
14. A strong need for improving the quality of Orientation Programmes and 
Refreshers Courses. 
15. Draw up its academic calendar providing for dates of admission, 
schedule of vacation, holding of examination and declaring of results, 
efforts should be made that such academic calendars are synchronized at 
least for universities within a state so that students are not put to any 
inconvenience in the event of mobility from one university to another, if 
the need so arises. 
16. A Cental Higher Educaton Tribunal be set up for expeditious disposal of 
litigations on service matters relating to both academic and non-academic 
staff in the higher education system.

MATHLA Programme by CBSE 
664. SHRI S.M. LALJAN BASHA: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether CBSE has introduced a programme called MATHLAB for the 
high school students all over the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is a fact that proper monitoring was not done for this 
programme; 
(d) the steps CBSE proposed to take to help students in government schools 
who face the same problems in some subjects as private schools; and 
(e) the steps proposed by CBSE to introduce innovative schemes for the 
students? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. As 
per the information furnished by Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE), 
the Board has introduced the concept of Mathematics laboratory for the students 
from class III to X. For classes III to VIII, the schools would integrate practical 
skills in Mathematics as a part of the learning process. At the Secondary level 
(class IX and X), the Board has allotted 20 marks for practical skills in 
Mathematics. 
(c) No, Sir. CBSE has developed a proper mechanism to monitor this 
programme periodically and has taken adequate measures before 
implementing this programme. Guidelines have been prepared for schools for 
setting up mathematics laboratories for classes III to IX in collaboration with the 
Homi Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, Mumbai. 
(d) To help the students in Government Schools, CBSE is interacting with 
the Department of Education of the Government of Delhi to empower the staff of 
the Directorate with required information for effective implementation of the 
programme followed by teachers' training programmes. 
(e) CBSE prepares the textual material s and guidelines for teachers and 
students followed by massive teachers training programme across the country 
for effective implementation of innovative schemes for students. 
79

668. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:

of foreign universities into the country; 
(b) whether it is a fact that AlCTE made it mandatory that foreign 
universities should comply with its rules and regulations; 
(c) if so, the details thereof: 
(d) whether it is also a fact that AlCTE should prescribe fee and intake for 
courses in foreign universities; and 
(e) If so, the reasons therefor ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALIASHRAF FATMI): (a) The All India Council 
for Technical Education (AlCTE) has issued the revised Regulations for Entry 
and Operation of Foreign Universities/Institutions imparting Technical Education 
in India vide notification dated May 16,2005.

Outlay for education 
672. SHRI S.P.M. SYED KHAN: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the outlay for education could not be increased to the 
desired level of 6 per cent of GDP, as  estimated by the National Policy on 
Education for many years; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; 
(c) the present percentage of GDP; and 
(d) the steps taken by Government to increase the outlay for education? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALIASHRAF FATMI): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) to (d) The National Common Minimum Programme (NCMP) of the 
Government pledges to raise public spending on education to at least 6% of GDP 
with at least half this amount being spent on the primary and secondary 
education sectors, in a phased manner. However, it has not so far been possible to 
achieve this level of expenditure due to constraint on resources and other 
competing priorities. An Education Cess has been imposed to fulfil the 
commitment of the Government to provide and finance the universalisation of 
quality basic education to children in the 6-14 years age-group. For the year 2005-
06, the total Plan allocation for the Department of Secondary & Higher Education 
and the Department of Elementary Education & Literacy has been stepped up 
to 15243.76 crore as against Rs.8225.00 crore in 2004-05. The bulk of the 
expenditure on education is incurred by the State Governments. The 
expenditure on education as percentage of GDP is estimated at 3.49% during 2004-
05 (advance estimate).

673. SHRIMATI JAMANA DEVI BARUPAL: 
DR. T SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the Central Advisory Board on Education met in the month of 
June, 2005 to discuss sweeping changes recommended in the private national 
curriculum frame work 2005; 
91 

RAJYA SABHA [1 August, 2005] 
(b) if so, whether the changes recommended by the CABE were practical; 
(c) if so, whether there are 43 education boards in the country and it is for 
them to implement the changes at the earliest; 
(d) if so, whether, the NCERT is an advisory body which has no role in 
implementing the recommendations made by the CABE; and 
(e) if so, the extent to which these reforms in education would help in 
removing the illiteracy in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALIASHRAF FATMI) :(a) to (e) The Central 
Advisory Board of Education (CABE) met on the 7th June, 2005 to discuss the 
draft National Curriculum Framework (NCF) 2005. The NCF includes the 
following salient features: 
(I) It is based on the following four guiding principles:— (i) Connecting 
knowledge of life outside the school, (ii) Ensuring that learning shifts 
away from rote methods, (iii) Enriching the curriculum so that it goes 
beyond textbooks, (iv) Making examinations more flexible. 
(II) The NCF also focuses on the child as an active learner, thus giving 
primacy to the children's experiences, their voices and their participation. 
It views children as active participants in the construction of knowledge, 
and states that schools should recognize the innate ability and creativity 
of each child to construct his/her own knowledge. 
(III) It recommends the softening of subject boundaries so that children can get 
a tast of integrated knowledge and joy of understanding. 
(IV) It reaffirms faith in panchayati raj institutions to enable people to think, 
decide and act in their collectiv e interest, to provide greater 
participation of people in development. 
The draft NCF, duly approved by the Executive Committee of the NCERT, was 
discussed in the meeting of the Central Advisory Board of Education (CABE) 
held on the 7th June, 2005 wherein it was decided that the draft NCF needed 
more wide ranging consultations. 
92 

[1 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
The NCF has been translated in the regional languages of Assamese, Bengali, 
Dogri, Gujarati, Kannada, Konkani, Malayaiam, Manipuri, Maithili, Marathi, 
Nepali, Oriya, Punjabi, Sanskrit, Tamil, and Telugu and translated versions have 
been sent to the respective State Governments and Organisations. State 
Governments were, in pursuance of decision taken in the CABE meeting, 
requested to initiate discussion among all stakeholders and convey their 
considered views to the CABE after which the draft will be discussed further and 
finalized in the next meeting of the CABE to be held in August 2005. 
The NCERT will prepare syllabi ba sed on the revised curriculum and 
thereafter, prepare textbooks in all subjects for all classes. 
The NCERT is an apex level body to provide educational resource support on 
issues relating to school education. Curriculum design has a special place 
among the diverse responsibilities envisaged in the charter of NCERT. 
The reforms envisaged in the NCF 2005 will go a long way in reducing the 
curricular burden on children, reducing inequality in the classrooms and 
making learning a more joyful and relevant experience. These measures are likely to 
impact dropout rates. With more and more children accessing and participating in 
the learning process, there will be a significant impact on literacy in the years to 
come.

712. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that various State Governments permitted setting-up of 
private universities; 
(b) whether such universities have also set-up their own subsidiary 
institutes in various other States and enrolled thousands of students to their 
various study programmes collecting exorbitant fees; 
(c) if so, the details in this regard; 
(d) whether the hon'ble Supreme Court recently struck down the law under 
which such private universities were se t-up as ultra vires of the Constitution; 
and 
(e) if so, the deails in this regard with fate of the students of the affected 
universities? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) to (e) The 
incorporation, regulation and winding up of Universities are within the 
competence of the State Legislatures. State Universities cannot setup off-
campus centres outside the jurisdiction of the respective States. According to 
the information furnished by the University Grants Commission (UGC), 
several private universities established in the State of Chhattisgarh under the 
Chhattisgarh Niji Kshetra Vishwavidyalaya (Sthapana Aur Viniyaman) 
Adhiniyam, 2002, had off-campus centres outside the State. The Supreme 
Court of India in its judgement in the Writ Petition (Civil) No. 19/2004: Prof. 
Yash Pal & Ors. Vs. State of Chhattisgarh & Ors., declared the provisions of 
the State Act permitting off-campus centres outside Chhattisgarh to be ultra 
vires of the Constitution. Thus the private universities established under the Act 
have ceased to exist. The Supreme Court directed that the State Government may 
take appropriate measures to have these institutions affiliated to 
126 

[1 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
the already existing State Universities in Chhattisgarh. It was further directed 
that the benefit of affiliation of an institution shall be extended only if it 
fulfills the requisite norms and standards laid down for such purpose and not 
to every kind of institution. Regarding technical, medical or dental colleges, etc. 
affiliation may be accorded if they have been established after fulf illing the 
prescribed criteria laid down by the All India Council of Technical Education 
(AICTE), Medical Council of India (MCI), Dental Council of India or any 
other statutory authority and with their approval or sanction as prescribed by 
law. 
The Central Government has requested all the State Governments to get the 
off-campus centres of the erstwhile private universities of Chhattisgarh located 
in their respective States, affiliated to the jurisdictional State Universities in order to 
protect the interests of the affected students studying in them.

726. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that recently some fresh initiatives have been taken to 
revive research and the study of basic sciences as, reportedly, outline by the 
M.M. Sharma task force, constituted in March, 2005 to make an assessment 
of the present status of scientific research and training in the universities and to 
determine the areas of concern; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof, including major recommendations made by the 
M.M. Sharma task force and the action taken/proposed to be taken thereon, 
alongwith their present status? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) to (b) A Task Force 
for basic scientific research in universities was set up by the Government with 
the following terms of reference: 
(i) To make an assessment of the present status of scientific research 
& training in Universities and to determine the areas of concern. 
(ii) To suggest solutions and strategies to retrieve and enhance the 
excellence of Universities in the area of scientific research and 
training. 
(iii) To make an assessment of the resources required both in physical and 
financial terms to implement these solutions and its modalities. 
The Task Force has mainly recommended that in order to promote quality 
scientific research in universities, infrastructural facilities ought to be upgraded 
by providing development grants for modern laboratories, physical infrastructure 
including uninterrupted power supply, water, safety requirements of international 
standards, high level equipment with built-in maintenance mechanism, 
exclusive research students' hostel and a research starter fund, need to create 
ten networking centres in Basic Sciences in leading departments of 
universities in different parts of the country to promote collaborative research, 
access to advanced facilities and imparting training in frontier areas, etc. The 
report of the Task Force

Guidelines for Publication of Foreign Journals and Facsimile editions of 
Foreign News papers on 01.8.2005 
Guidelines for 
(i)   Publication of Newspapers and Periodicals dealing with News and 
Current Affairs. 
(ii)   Publication of Facsimile Editions of Foreign Newspapers. 
New Delhi, Dated 13th 
July, 2005. 
PREAMBLE 
In supersession of the previous guidelines issued by this Ministry vide Press 
Note dated 21st November 2002 and in partial modification of the Press Note 
dated 5th July 2005, the Union Government have decided to allow, with 
immediate effect: 
155 

RAJYA SABHA [1 August, 2005] 
(i) Foreign Direct Investment (which includes foreign direct investments 
by NRIs, PIOs) and portfolio investments by recognized Flls, together 
up to a ceiling of 26% of paid up equity capital, in Indian entities 
publishing newspapers and periodicals dealing with news and 
current affairs. Such investment would be permissible by foreign 
entities having sound credentials and international standing, subject 
to certain conditions. 
(ii) Facsimile editions, in whole or in part(s), of foreign newspapers, 
by Indian entities, with or without foreign investment, and also by 
foreign companies owning the original newspaper, provided they get 
incorporated and registered in India under the Companies Act, 
1956. 
The following guidelines are hereby prescribed: 
1. Application 
(i) Nine copies of the prescribed application form, duly filled in, 
along with the requisite documents shall be submitted to the 
Ministry of l&B. 
(ii) Application fee of Rs. 5000/- will have to be submitted through 
demand draft made in favour of Pay & Accounts Officer, Ministry of 
Information and Broadcasting, payable at New Delhi. 
2. Title of the Publication 
Title verification shall continue to be done by the Press Registrar as per 
existing procedure, including for facsimile editions. 
3. Eligibility Criteria 
A. Foreign Investment in Indian entities publishing newspapers and 
periodicals dealing with news and current affairs: 
(i) Foreign Investment will be allowed only where the resultant entity 
(hereinafter called "New Entity"') is a company registered with the 
Registrar of Companies under the provisions of the Companies 
Act, 1956. 
(ii) Foreign Investment including FDI by foreign entites, NRIs, PIOs etc. 
and portfolio investments by recognised Flls, will be allowed up to 
maximum of 26% of paid-up equity of the New entity. 
156 

[1 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(iii) Permission will be granted only in cases where equity held by the 
largest Indian shareholder is at least 51% of the paid up equity, 
excluding the equity held by Public Sector Banks and Public 
Financial Institutions as defined in Section 4A of the Companies 
Act, 1956, in the New Entity. The term largest Indian shareholder used 
in this clause will include any or a combination of the following: 
(1) In the case of an individual shareholder, 
(a) The individual shareholder 
(b) A relative of the shareholder within the meaning of section 6 of the 
Companies Act, 1956 
(c) A company/group of companies in which the individual share-
holder/H U F to which he belongs, has management and 
controlling interest. 
(2) In the case of an Indian company, 
(a) The Indian company, 
(b) A group of Indian companies under the same management and 
ownership control. Provided that in case of a combination of all or 
any of the entities mentioned in sub-clause (1) and (2) above, each 
of the parties shall have entered into a legally binding agreement to 
act as a single unit in managing the matters of the New Entity. 
(iv) While calculating the 26% foreign investment in the equity of the 
New Entity, the foreign holding component, if any, in the equity 
for the Indian shareholder companies of the New Entity will be duly 
reckoned on pro rata basis so as to arrive at the total foreign 
holding in the New Entity. 
(v) At least 50% of the foreign direct investment will have to be 
inducted by issue of fresh equity. The balance, viz. upto 50% of the 
foreign direct investment, may be inducted through transfer of 
existing equity. 
(vi) Permission would be conditional on at least 3/4th of the Directors on 
the Board of Directors of the New Entity and all key executives 
and editorial staff being resident Indians. 
157 

RAJYA SABHA [1 August, 2005]  
B. Facsimile Editions of foreign newspapers: 
(i) Any Indian entity, with or without foreign investment, desirous of 
publishing a facsimile edition of a foreign newspaper, or any foreign 
company owning the original foreign newspaper will be permitted to 
publish the facsimile edition of its newspaper, in whole or in 
part(s), provided: 
(a) it is incorporated and registered as a company with the 
Registrar of Companies unde r the provisions of the 
Companies Act, 1956. 
(b) It has a commercial presence in India with its principal place of 
business in India. 
(c) That a least 3/4th of the Directors on the Board of Directors of the 
New Entity and all key executives and editorial staff are 
resident Indians. 
(ii) Any entity publishing a facsimile edition of a foreign newspaper in 
India shall be subject to all th e relevant laws and guidelines 
applicable to Indian newspapers and their publishers. 
4. Basic Conditions/Obligations: 
(i) Subject to the ceiling prescribed, it will be obligatory on the part 
of the all Entities to inform Ministry of Information & 
Broadcasting about any alteration in the foreign shareholding pattern 
as on 31st March of every year and within 15 days of the end of 
the financial year. 
(ii) It will be obligatory on the part of all entities to take prior 
permission from the Ministry of Information & Broadcasting 
before effecting any changes in the shareholding of the largest Indian 
shareholder indicated in clause 3A (iii) above. 
(iii) AH entities shall inform Ministry of Information & Broadcasting 
within 15 days of effecting any change in the composition of its Board 
of Directors or key executives and editorial staff. Such a change would 
be subject to post-facto approval of the Ministry of Information & 
Broadcasting. 
(iv) All entities shall obtain prior clearance of the Ministry of 
Information & Broadcasting of any foreigners/NRIs proposed to 
158 

[1 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
be employed/engaged in the New Entity either as consultants (or in any other 
capacity) for more than 60 days in a year, or, as regular employees. 
(v) Facsimile editions shall be permitted subject to the following conditions: 
(a) The original foreign newspaper, whose facsimile edition is proposed to be brought 
out in India, is being published with the approval of the regulatory authority of the 
country of origin and is a standard publication in that country and is not specially designed 
for Indian readers. 
(b) The facsimile edition shall not carry any advertisements aimed at Indian readers 
in any form, 
(c) The fascimile edition shall not carry any locally generated content/ India specific 
content, which is not simultaneously published in the original edition of foreign newspaper, 
(d) Prior permission from Ministry of l&B is obtained for publication of facsimile 
editions and the title got registered with the Registrar of Newspapers for India (RNI). 
(e) The publication shall clearly indicate that it is a facsimile edition, in whole or in 
part(s), and shall prominently carry the mast head, the editorial page and the place of 
publication of the original foreign newspaper. 
5. Processing of Applications 
(i) All new applications for foreign investments in Indian entities publishing 
newspapers and periodicals dealing with news and current affairs and proposals for 
publishing of facsimile editions of foreign newspapers, shall be processed and 
decided upon in the Ministry of information & Broadcasting on the basis of inter-
ministerial consultation with the Ministry of Home Affairs and other 
ministries, as may be required. 
(ii) The applicant entity shall make full disclosure, at the time of application, of 
Shareholders' Agreements and Loan Agreements that are finalized or proposed to 
be entered into. Any subsequent change in these shall be disclosed to the Ministry 
of Information & Broadcasting within fifteen days of such a change. 
(iii) The applicant entity shall frame its Articles/Memorandum of 
159

Association to ensure compliance with the prescribed eligibility criteria. 

(iv) All entities shall obtain prior clearance from the Ministry of Information & 
Broadcasting of all persons not being resident Indians who are proposed to be 
inducted in the Board of Directors of the new Entity. 
(v) All applications for publishing facsimile editions shall clearly indicate whether 
the facsimile edition is to be published in whole or in part. In case only a part of 
the original foreign newspaper is proposed to be published, each page shall be 
treated as one part, and the exact page numbers of the original foreign newspaper

Advertisement of liquor and 
cigarettes 
741. SHRI PRAMOD MAHAJAN: Will the Minister of INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state the steps Government are taking to 
prevent surrogate advertisements about liquor and/or cigarettes? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI S. 
JAIPAL REDDY) Advertisements on TV channels transmitted/retransmitted 
through Cable Network are required to adhere to the Advertising Code 
prescribed vide Rule 7 of Cable Television Networks Rules 1994, which, inter-
alia, provides that no advertisment shall be permitted which promotes directly to 
indirectly production, sale or consumption of cigarette, tobacco, wine, alcohol, 
liquor or other intoxicants. Channels distributed through DTH are also 
required to adhere to this Code. 
All India Radio and Doordarshan follow their own Code for Commercial 
Advertising which prohibits advertisements of cigarettes and tobacco products. 
Private FM Radio channels are required to adhere to the AIR Code. 
Under Section 19 of Cable Television Networks (Regulation)Act 1995, an 
authorized officer i.e. District Magistrate or Sub Divisional Magistrate or 
Commissioner of Police can take action for violations of the Codes. Further, 
The Central Government has constituted an Inter-Ministerial Committee to 
look into violations of the Advertising Code by various TV Channels. 
172 

[1 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA  
A circular has been issued on 12.04.2005 to all TV channels asking them to 
strictly adhere to Rule 7(2)(viii) of the Advertising Code, which prohibits 
advertisement of tobacco/liquor. 
The Press Council of India (PCI) is a statutory autonomous self-regulatory 
body set up under the Press Council Act, 1978 with twin object of "preserving the 
freedom of the press" and of "maintaining and improving the standards of 
newspapers and news agencies in India". As per subsection 2(c) of the Press 
Council Act, 1978; the Council is required to ensure on the part of the 
newspapers, news agencies and journalists, the maintenance of high standards of 
public taste and foster a due sense of both the rights and responsibilities or 
citizenship. Accordingly, PCI has "Norms of Journalistic Conduct" which, 
inter alia, state that "No advertisement shall be published which promotes 
directly or indirectly, production/sale or consumption of cigarettes, tobacco 
products, wine, alcohol, liquor and any other intoxicants". 
The Cigarettes and other Toba cco Products (Prohibitions of 
Advertisement and Regulation of-Trade and Commerce, Production, Supply and 
Distribution) Act, 2004 prohibits advertisements of cigarettes or any other 
tobacco products. Rules framed there under have been amended vide notification 
dated 31.05.2005 to introduce a clear definition of indirect advertisement, which, 
inter alia, includes ban on advertisement of non-tobacco products bearing the 
same brand as of tobacco product, the use of particular colours, lay out and/or 
presentation associated with the particular tobacco product.

PREAMBLE 
In supersession of the previous guidelines issued by this Ministry vide Press 
Note dated 21st November, 2002 and in partial modification of the Press Note 
dated 5th July 2005, the Union Government have decided to allow, with 
immediate effect: 
(i) Foreign Direct Investment (which includes foreign direct investments

Flls, together up to a ceiling of 26% of paid up equity capital, in 
Indian entities publishing newspapers  and periodicals dealing with 
news and current affairs. Such investment would be permissible by 
foreign entities having sound credentials and international standing, 
subject to certain conditions. 
(ii) Facsimile editions, in whole or in part(s), of foreign newspapers, by 
Indian entities, with or without foreign investment, and also by foreign 
companies owning the original newspaper, provided they get 
incorporated and registered in India under the Companies Act, 1956. 
The following guidelines are hereby prescribed: 
1. Application 
(i) Mine copies of the prescribed application form, duly filled in, along 
with the requisite documents shall be submitted to the Ministry of 
l&B. 
(ii) Application fee of Rs. 5000/- will have to be submitted through 
demand draft made in favour of Pay & Accounts Officer, Ministry of 
Information and Broadcasting, payable at New Delhi. 
2. Title of the Publication  
Title verification shall continue to be done by the Press Registrar as per 
existing procedure, including for facsimile editions. 
3. Eligibility Criteria 
A. Foreign Investment in Indian entities publishing newspapers and 
periodicals dealing with news and current affairs: 
(i) Foreign Investment will be allowed only where the resultant entity 
(hereinafter called "New Entity)") is  a company registered with the 
Registrar of Companies under the provisions of the Companies Act, 1956. 
(ii) Foreign Investment including FDI by foreign entities, NRIs, PIOs etc. 
and portfolio investments by recognized Flls, will be allowed up to a 
maximum of 26% of paid-up equity of the New Entity. 
175 

RAJYA SABHA [1 August, 2005] 
(iii) Permission will be granted only in cases where equity held by the largest 
Indian shareholder is at least 51% of the paid up equity, excluding the 
equity held by Public Sector Banks and Public Financial Institutions 
as defined in Section 4A of the Companies Act, 1956, in the New 
Entity. The term largest Indian shareholder used in this clause w ill 
include any or a combination of the following: 
(1) In the case of an individual shareholder, 
a) The individual shareholder 
b) A relative of the shareholder within the meaning of section 6 of the 
Companies Act, 1956 
c) A company/group of companies in which the individual 
shareholder/HUF to which he belongs, has management and 
controlling interest 
(2) In the case of an Indian company, 
a) The Indian company 
b) A group of Indian companies under the same management and 
ownership control. 
Provided that in case of a combination of all or any of the entities 
mentioned in sub-clause (1) and (2) above, each of the parties shall have entered 
into a legally binding agreement to act as a single unit in managing the matters of 
the New Entity. 
(iv) While calculating the 26% foreign investment in the equity of the 
New Entity, the foreign holding component, if any, in the equity of 
the Indian Shareholder companies of the New Entity will be duly 
reckoned on pro rata basis so as to arrive at the total foreign 
holding in the New Entity. 
(v) At least 50% of the foreign direct investment will have to be 
inducted by issue of fresh equity. The balance, viz. upto 50% of the 
foreign direct investment, may be inducted through transfer of 
existing equity.

[1 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(vi) Permission would be conditional on at least 3/4th of the Directors on the

editorial staff being resident Indians. 
B. Facsimile Editions newspapers: 
(i) Any Indian entity, with or without foreign investment, desirous of 
publishing a facsimile edition of a fo reign newspaper, or any foreign 
company owning the original foreign newspaper will be permitted to 
publish the facsimile edition of its newspaper, in whole or in part(s), 
provided

Registrar of Companies under the provisions of the companies 
Act, 1956.

resident Indians.

Indian newspapers and their publishers. 
4. Basic Conditions/Obligations 
(i) Subject to the ceiling prescribed, it will be obligatory on the part of 
the all Entities to inform Ministry of Information & Broadcasting about 
any alteration in the foreign shareholding pattern as on 31st March of 
every year and within 15 days of the end of the financial year. 
(ii) It will be obligatory on the part of the all entities to take prior 
permission from the Ministry of Information & Broadcasting before 
effecting any changes in the shar eholding of the largest Indian 
shareholder indicated in clause 3A (iii) above.

Board of Directors or key executives and editorial staff. Such a

Vacations in court 
753. SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that civil courts in lower Judiciary combined with High 
Courts and Supreme Court are the only constitutional institutions to observe 
summer and winter vacations; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that hundreds of thousands of court cases are 
pending and that their number shows no signs of abating; 
(c) whether in view of (a) and (b) above, Government would consider to put an 
end to the colonial practice of courts observing summer vacations; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LAW AND 
JUSTICE (SHRI K. VENKATAPATHY): (a) to (d) The working days in the 
Supreme Court and High Courts are regulated by the rules framed by the 
respective Courts. According to available information, the Supreme Court of 
India works for 222 days in a year; all High Courts in the country normally 
have 210 working days in a year and the number of working days of the 
District/Subordinate Courts are regulated by the concerned High Court. 
The question of curtailing/discontinuing the vacations in the Courts has been 
considered in the past, but it has not been found feasible or advisable to do so 
because of the taxing nature of work of the Judiciary and the Bar. The Department 
of Justice in July 2001 had invited the views of the High Courts regarding the 
number of working days in the High Courts and the curtailment of their 
vacations. Replies were received from 14 High Courts. The High Court of 
Uttaranchal increased the number of its working days in a year from 210 to 224 
and the High Court of karnataka from 210 to 214. Jharkhand High Court had no 
objection to increase the number of working days. Other High Courts had not 
favoured increase in the number of their working days in a year. 
In view of the urgent need of the hour to reduce the huge pendencies 
prevailing in the High Courts, this Department addressed to all the High 
Courts, requesting them to fix the period of vacations in such a way that the 
number of working days of High Courts generally do not fall below 222 days in a 
year. 
189 

RAJYA SABHA [1 August, 2005]  
Various other steps have been taken by the Government-to expedite disposal 
of cases, these include periodically monitoring the pendency position in courts, 
grouping of cases involving common question of law, constitution of specialized 
benches, timely filling up the vacancies of judges, increasing the judge strength, 
organizing Lok Adalats at regular intervals, encouraging alternative modes of 
disputes resolution like negotiation, mediation and arbitration and setting up of 
special tribunals like Central Administrative Tribunals, State Administrative 
Tribunals, Income Tax Appellate Tribunals, Family Courts, Labour Courts etc.

770. SHRI V. HANUMANTHA RAO: Will the Minister of SOCIAL 
JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that there is a need of trained people,

(b) the existing Government organizations/institutions which offer courses

challenged persons;

(a) and (b) Recognizing the need for trained professionals for giving services to 
persons with mental retardation, a National Institute for the Mentally 
Handicapped was set up at Hyderabad in 1984 to develop professionals, 
preparation of service modules and conduct research and development in the field 
of mental retardation. The Government has also established Rehabilitation 
Council of India in 1986 subsequently made it a statutory body in 1992 to 
standardize the courses, ensure quality in the programmes and regulate 
rehabilitation professionals and personnel.

professionals. Besides, 77,298 professionals have been given continuing 
education programmes. RCI has recognized 185 organisations including

the field of mental retardation.

772. SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: Will the Minister of TRIBAL AFFAIRS 
be pleased to state: 
(a)whether Government are aware that a few self-proclaimed 
environmental groups are deliberately misrepresenting the Tribal Bill initiative as a 
move to convert state property into property of the tribals terming them as 
encroachers and criminals; 
(b) whether sixty per cent of the country's dense forests are found around 
the Adivasi settlements which works as a hub for conservation of nature and 
critical for their cultural and material survival; and 
(c) whether Government would ensure protection to the tribals who have an 
inalienable stake in the forests? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI P.R. KYNDIAH): (a) The 
Ministry of Tribal Affairs has been mandated to formulate a comprehensive Central 
Legislation to redress the historical injustice done to forest dwelling Scheduled 
Tribes by providing for clear assertion of their legal rights on land and other 
traditional forest rights. The Ministry of Tribal Affairs has prepared a draft. 
"The Scheduled Tribes (Recognition of Forest Rights) Bill, 2005", to 
provide a legislative frame for recognition of the aforementioned rights, 
in consultation with the concerned Ministries, including the Ministry of 
Law and Justice. 
The bill was posted on the website of the Ministry of Tribal Affairs seeking 
comments/suggestions from the members of the public, the social activists, 
academicians, anthropologists, the experts working for the cause of 
environmental protection and welfare of tribal people and other stakeholders on the 
proposed legislation till 10.07.2005.  The Ministry has received 
comments/suggestions from a large number of individuals/organizations, either 
supporting the Bill or opposing the same on various grounds. 
(b) As per the State Forests Report, 2003, about 63% of dense forest cover 
of the country lies in 187 tribal districts.

the established procedure taking views and comments received from the 
stakeholders into consideration.

velopment Scheme for Mega Cities (covering infrastructure projects for 5

Schemes for urban poor in Uttar Pradesh 
†793. PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: Will the Minister of URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the programmes and schemes formulated and to be 
implemented by Government to provide necessary amenities to the poor living 
in small and big cities of Uttar Pradesh during the last three years; and 
(b) the details of the amount sanctioned, district-wise or city-wise by 
Government during this period and the amount spent by the State 
Government in this connection? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (KUMARI SELJA): (a) 
and (b) The Ministry of Urban Employment & Poverty Alleviation is mainly 
implementing two schemes related to providing necessary amenities to the 
urban poor (living in slum areas) viz. Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana 
(VAMBAY) and National Slum Development Programme (NSDP) during the 
last three years. In addition, an employment oriented urban poverty alleviation 
programme namely Swarna Jayanti Shah ari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY) is also 
being implemented by the Ministry to ameliorate the conditions of the urban 
poor by providing them gainful employment & skill upgradation. 
The objective of VAMBAY is to provide shelter or upgrade the existing 
shelter for the people living below the poverty line in urban slums and also to 
provide healthy and enabling urban environment through community 
sanitation. 
The objective of NSDP was to provide water supply, sanitation, primary 
education, adult literacy, health care, environment improvement and 
community empowerment for the population living in slums, the NSDP stands 
discontinued w.e.f. 1.4.2005. SJSRY strives to provide gainful employment to 
the urban unemployed poor through setting up of micro enterprises and also 
through provision of wage employment by utilizing their labour for 
construction of useful public assets.

SHRI TARLOCHAN SINGH (Haryana): Sir, I rise to make a Special 
Mention about the Parsi Community which is one of the five minority 
communities recognised by the Government of India. They have made a 
unique contribution in the country's development, especially, in the field of

real plight of this community. The National Commission for Minorities had

legislatures of Maharashtra and Gujarat. This can be done without 
amending the Constitution and a healthy convention can be started within 
the existing provisions. The Ministry  of Health also may devote proper 
attention to the genetic problems of this community and to open pro-
fertility clinics. I further request that the Government of India may make 
special provisions for celebrations of the Parsi New Year which falls on

Discharge of oily substance in the Beaches of Goa 
SHRI SHANTARAM NAIK (Goa): On  26th July, an oily substance 
deposited along the coastline in the Salcete taluka of Goa from Mobor 
beach to the Benaulim beach was seen by the villagers. There is a difference 
of opinion as to whether the substance was tar balls or raw oil. The Director 
so Science and Technology in Goa opined that the substance was raw oil 
discharged only recently from a nearby place, say, from Karwa or 20 kms. 
away from Goa. Whatever may be the nature of the substance, it had the 
effect of polluting beautiful and clean beaches of Goa, although to a lesser 
extent. It is also not clear as to how such a mischievous discharge of 
polluting substance was not noticed by the Coast Guard. This type of 
blatant rape of Goa beaches should not go unpunished. The Union Ministry 
of Environment has to chalk out a plan in coordination with the State 
Governments for the protection of beaches in the country. Although the 
Environment Protection Act and the laws relating to air and water pollution 
have enough provisions to deal with such situations, yet it is clear that the 
Enforcement Agencies are not efficient enough. The Indian Coast Guard 
has to be vigilant not merely with respect to the instruction of 
unauthorised ships or other illegal movements on our coastline but they 
have to nab those who discharge dangerous substances in the sea to the 
detriment of human and marine lives. The Government should investigate 
as to whether there was any conspiracy to spoil the Goan beaches to 
get the tourist traffic diverted to other countries.

Having said that, let me just pick up one sentence from the hon. Home 
Minister's statement made this afternoon. It was very brief and correctly 
so. This was the statement that the Legislative Assembly was dissolved 
on the 23rd of May, 2005. Now, Sir, I am convinced, as a lawyer and as a 
citizen, that a dissolved body is a dead body, and giving oxygen to a dead 
body cannot revive it. Only Court can perform a miracle. I have been in the 
profession now almost 55 years and I am never surprised at what miracles 
Courts can perform, especially when there is a minority coalition 
Government at the Centre. Sir, what happens after dissolution? I, therefore, 
leave it to the wisdom or inventive capacities of our,activist Court. I only 
wish to say a few words about what is the Constitutional position before 
dissolution because after dissolution it is beyond the powers of anybody 
else. Sir, one important thing that we must know is that the Governor— 
and we are just now speaking only of the Governor—is bound by the 
advice of his Council of Ministers just like the King in England is bound, 
and he follows the same set of principles, save and except in the matter of 
a dissolution, he has a small area of discretion, and that area of discretion 
is, he must not foist upon the electorate another election if it is possible to 
have a political party forming a Government. That is a well-known 
convention. It is one of the silences of our Constitution. It is known as a 
convention in our Constitution. That power of dissolution when a President's 
Rule is imposed, is vested in the President obviously. I find that there was 
no opportunity given to the President who was the deciding authority, the 
feeling that I had, and many people in this country also had, was that the 
absence of the President was used in order to have this dissolution. I may 
be wrong and, therefore, I would only like to know, Sir, very, importantly

a majority. When did that happen? It happened when the margin between 
the number of members who formed the Government and the number of

Governments were formed. That is why we said that if a party does not 
have a full majority, but it comes forward and says that they would form a 
Government and if the Governor in his subjective opinion comes to the 
conclusion that such a Government could continue, they could be allowed 
to form a Government. While criticising the Resolution, the fact which the
